slides.title: Genetic Rescue & Assisted Gene Flow
slides.storyContext: Dr. Nair discusses new conservation tools: 'We can capture wild tigers from one reserve, breed them in captivity, and release their offspring to another isolated reserve. This introduces genetic diversity without moving wild animals.'

points.label: Genetic Rescue
points.text: Introducing new alleles into an inbred population by crossing with individuals from another population. Can restore fitness, reduce inbreeding depression. Risky if introduced alleles are locally maladapted.

points.label: Assisted Gene Flow
points.text: Intentional translocation of individuals between reserves to increase connectivity. Less disruptive than physical corridors; allows single-step rescue. Requires careful genetic matching (maximize diversity, minimize maladaptation).

points.label: Limitations
points.text: May introduce diseases; cultural mismatch if different tiger subpopulations have distinct behaviors. Works only if source population is itself healthy; can't rescue extremely low populations.

slides.inSimpleWords: Isolated tiger reserves can swap individuals to mix genes. This stops inbreeding even without building physical corridors.

slides.title: The Rescued Rhino: When Science Saves Species
slides.storyContext: Priya reads about Arabian oryx: 'In 1972, only 9 individuals remained (3 in captivity, 6 wild). The species was declared functionally extinct. Today, 1,000+ live in the wild. How? Captive breeding + reintroduction. Humans brought a species back from the brink.'

slides.title: CITES & International Conservation Law
slides.storyContext: Rajesh explains: 'Global agreement signed in 1973 — CITES. Banned trading endangered species (tigers, rhinos, elephant ivory). India ratified it. Now, if someone smuggles tiger skin, it's an international crime, not just local theft.'

points.label: CITES Structure
points.text: Appendix I: species threatened with extinction (ban trade). Appendix II: species that may become threatened (trade allowed only if sustainable). Appendix III: species protected by ≥1 nation. 183 nations signed; covers ~38,000 species.

points.label: Effectiveness
points.text: Reduced trade in giant pandas, Arabian oryx, Indian rhinos. Limited by weak enforcement in source countries, high black-market demand, corruption. Estimates: illegal wildlife trade = $23 billion/year globally.

points.label: Limitations
points.text: Focuses on trade; doesn't address habitat loss. Can perversely increase value (scarcity → premium price → more poaching). Some species delisted when poaching resumed.

slides.inSimpleWords: Global law says: don't buy endangered animals. Breaks supply chain. Works only if countries enforce it and poachers fear jail.

slides.title: The Ivory Ban That Wasn't Enough
slides.storyContext: Priya researches: 'CITES banned ivory trade in 1989. Elephant poaching dropped initially. But illegal trade resumed in 2000s; bribes allowed smuggling through ports. Today, 20,000+ elephants killed yearly for ivory. A law without enforcement is just words.'

slides.title: Conservation Priorities & Triage
slides.storyContext: Dr. Nair explains difficult decisions: 'We can't save every species. Limited budget. We prioritize: species with highest extinction risk (CR), species most important to ecosystem (keystone), species with best chance of recovery (high resilience).'

points.label: Triage Strategy
points.text: Rank species by extinction risk (IUCN category), ecological role (keystone species), and recovery probability. Save high-risk + high-impact + high-recovery first. Leave resilient, low-impact species for later.

points.label: Keystone Species
points.text: Species with disproportionate impact on ecosystem structure/function. Example: sea otters (control sea urchins, which otherwise overgraze kelp). Protecting keystone species protects whole ecosystem.

points.label: Umbrella Species
points.text: Large-range species whose habitat protection benefits many co-occurring species. Tigers are umbrella species: protecting tiger corridors protects hundreds of smaller species using the same forest.

slides.inSimpleWords: Save the most endangered first. Save species that support many others. Save species we can actually recover. That's how to maximize species saved per dollar.

slides.title: Keystone or Icon? The Tiger's Double Role
slides.storyContext: Dr. Nair explains: 'Tigers are iconic — charismatic megafauna, emotional draw, fundraising power. But they're also keystone predators. Their territories create a network of protected forests. Save tigers, save forests, save 100+ species that live there. That's why we invest in tiger conservation despite limited resources.'

slides.title: Climate Adaptation & Assisted Migration
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'If climate warms and species can't migrate, do we move them manually?' Dr. Nair nods: 'Assisted migration is controversial but increasingly necessary. The Nilgiri tahr can't climb higher; the peak is the limit. We're studying whether we can establish populations on cooler mountains elsewhere.'

points.label: Assisted Migration (Rewilding)
points.text: Intentional translocation of species to new ranges to escape climate change or lost habitat. Controversial: may introduce species to ecosystems they didn't evolve with, disrupt local species, spread parasites. Requires evidence of suitability.

points.label: Climate Refuge Identification
points.text: High-elevation mountains, deep forests, wetland complexes: places with cooler microclimates or natural insulation. Prioritize these for protection as climate refugia. Example: Western Ghats' montane regions (high elevation = cooler) are critical for species tracking climate upslope.

points.label: Limits to Adaptation
points.text: Some species can't adapt genetically fast enough (long generation time). Some can't disperse (habitat fragmentation). Some depend on co-evolved species (pollinator-plant mutualism) that can't migrate together. These 'losers' may face inevitable extinction despite conservation effort.

slides.inSimpleWords: As climate warms, we might need to move species to cooler places. Risky, but extinction is riskier. We're learning to do this carefully.

slides.title: Recap: Biodiversity & Conservation
slides.storyContext: As Dr. Nair, Priya, and Rajesh stand on a hilltop overlooking the Western Ghats — green, alive, full of invisible species — they understand the urgency and the hope.

points.label: Biodiversity Levels
points.text: Genetic (allele diversity), species (richness + evenness), ecosystem (habitat variety). All three matter for resilience.

points.label: Hotspots
points.text: 2.4% of land holds 75% of threatened species. Prioritizing hotspots is cost-effective conservation.

points.label: Extinction Risk
points.text: IUCN categories (CR, EN, VU) guide conservation urgency. Habitat loss is the #1 cause; climate change rising fast.

points.label: MVP & Corridors
points.text: Species need minimum population size and habitat connectivity to survive. Isolated populations inbreed and crash.

points.label: Ex-Situ & In-Situ
points.text: Captive breeding (backup), wild protected areas (long-term). Both needed; neither alone is sufficient.

points.label: Community & Indigenous Knowledge
points.text: Sacred groves and community conservation protect 40% of Earth's biodiversity. Partnership with local people is key to success.

slides.inSimpleWords: Life on Earth is vanishing faster than we can count it. But with protected areas, corridors, captive backup, and community partnership, we can save most species. The choice is ours, the time is now.
